name: Zeús
tagline: Lord of the Sky · Wielder of the Thunderbolt
pronunciation: 'ZDEWS' — one syllable, beginning with a buzzing 'zd' and ending in a sharp 's', like the sound of distant thunder compressed into a name.
mythLead: The mythology of Zeús is dominated by two great struggles: his overthrow of the Titans and his defense of cosmic order against every subsequent threat. He is the last son of Kronos, the only one not swallowed at birth, and nearly every Greek cosmogony moves toward his throne.

myths.title: Hidden in a Cretan Cave
myths.text: Kronos swallowed each of his children at birth, convinced by a prophecy that a son would dethrone him. Rhea, pregnant with her youngest, appealed to her parents Gaia and starry Ouranos, who hid the infant Zeus in a cave 'in the rich land of Crete' (Hesiod, Theogony 453–491). To deceive Kronos, Rhea wrapped a great stone in swaddling clothes; he gulped it down, supposing he had swallowed Zeus. The child grew rapidly…

myths.title: The Ten Years' War for the Cosmos
myths.text: Grown to strength, Zeus forced Kronos to disgorge his siblings — Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon, with the stone disgorged last — and led the younger gods in a war against the Titans that raged for ten full years, 'a terrible battle' in which neither side could prevail (Hesiod, Theogony 617–735). The Cyclopes armed Zeus with thunder and lightning, Poseidon with the trident, Hades with the cap of…

myths.title: Typhôn and the Test of Sovereignty
myths.text: Even after the Titans fell, Gaia bore one final challenger: Typhôn, a hundred-headed, fire-breathing monster before whom the gods fled in terror to Egypt, all except Athena (Hesiod, Theogony 820–868). Zeus met him alone, hurling thunderbolts until the sea boiled and the mountains burned, then cast him down to Tartaros; in later tradition the monster lies pinned beneath Mount Etna, and the volcano's eruptions are his…

name: Hēra
tagline: The Golden-Throned · Guardian of Marriage
pronunciation: 'HAY-rah' — the first syllable is sharp and pitched; the final 'a' is long and open.
mythLead: Hēra's myths are almost all variations on one theme: the wronged wife defending her throne. She cannot overthrow Zeús, but she can punish his lovers and their children with relentless ingenuity — and beneath the vengeance the sources preserve traces of a far older, cosmic Hēra.

myths.title: The Cuckoo and the Daedala
myths.text: Greek tradition set the wooing of Hēra at Plataea in Boeotia. Pausanias (9.2.7–9.3.8) describes the local festival of the Daedala, at which wooden images were dressed as brides and burned on Mount Cithaeron — reenacting, the Plataeans said, the very origin of marriage: Zeús, unable to win the angry, aloof Hēra, had a wooden image dressed and carried in wedding procession; Hēra stormed up to tear the bride apart,…

myths.title: The Persecution of Hēraklēs
myths.text: Hēra's most famous feud is with Hēraklēs, living proof of Zeús's adultery with the mortal Alkmene. She sent two serpents to his cradle, and the infant strangled both (Pindar, Nemean 1.33–72). Years later she drove him to the madness in which he killed his own wife and children, and it was her will, working through Eurystheus, that imposed the Twelve Labors (Euripides, Heracles; Apollodorus 2.4.12). Yet the feud is…

myths.title: Argos Panoptês
myths.text: When Zeús desired the Argive princess Io, Hēra could not punish her husband — so she punished the beloved. Zeús turned Io into a cow; Hēra took the cow and set it under guard, and the guard she chose was Argos Panoptês, 'the all-seeing' — a giant with a hundred eyes that never all slept at once (Apollodorus 2.1.3; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.568–723). name: Poseidōn
tagline: The Earth-Shaker · Master of Waves
pronunciation: 'poh-SAY-done' — the second syllable is light, the third is long, pitched, and powerful.
mythLead: Poseidôn's myths dramatize the rage of the excluded. He is a great Olympian, co-equal of Zeus by lot, yet he is repeatedly thwarted — by Athena at Athens, by Odysseus after the blinding of Polyphemos, by the very mortals whose sacrifices he demands. His stories are the Greek meditation on power that cannot get what it wants.

myths.title: Lord of the Sea by Lot
myths.text: When the Titans fell, the three sons of Kronos divided the cosmos not by combat but by lot — a detail Homer preserves in Poseidon's own indignant speech. Zeus drew the sky, Hades the murky darkness, and Poseidon the grey sea, where he rules among his wife Amphitrite and the old sea gods; the earth and high Olympus were left in common (Iliad 15.187–193; Hesiod, Theogony 881–885). The arrangement makes Poseidon…

myths.title: Defeated by Athena at Athens
myths.text: Poseidon and Athena competed for the patronage of Attica, and their contest marks the Acropolis still. He struck the rock with his trident and produced a salt spring — or, in some tellings, the first horse — while Athena planted the olive tree, the first of the 'contest olive' whose descendant was shown to visitors for centuries (Pseudo-Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1; Herodotus 8.55; Pausanias 1.24.5). mythLead: Athénā's myths center on intelligence overcoming force. She is born from Zeus's head fully armed, defeats Poseidôn by gift rather than combat, and guides the heroes who win by cunning. Wherever she appears, calculation replaces rage.

Fighting for the Trojans, Árēs encounters the Greek Diomedes, into whom Athēnâ has poured strength and, most insulting, clear sight — the vision that lets a mortal look straight at gods. myths.text: In the song of Demodocus (Odyssey 8.266–366), Hēphaistos discovers his wife Aphrodítē in bed with Árēs — because the all-seeing Hēlios tells him. The smith rigs invisible bonds, ‘fine as spiders’ webs, of forged adamant,’ over the bed, pretends to leave for Lemnos, and catches the lovers mid-embrace. He calls the gods to witness, and the immortals gather to laugh: Hermês admits he would trade places with Árēs even…

myths.title: The First Murder Trial on the Areopagus
myths.text: A genuinely archaic myth makes Árēs the defendant in history’s first murder trial. Poseidôn’s son Halirrhothius raped Árēs’s daughter Alkippe; Árēs killed him on the spot and was charged by the sea-god before the assembled gods. mythLead: Hermês's myths celebrate intelligence in motion. Born at dawn, by nightfall he has invented music, stolen a herd, and talked his way out of both — and Zeús rewards him with every boundary-crossing office: herald, trader, guide of the dead. Every threshold in the Greek world — door, road, market, grave — stood under his sign.

myths.title: Born in a Cave on Mount Cyllene
myths.text: The Homeric Hymn to Hermes (1–104) stages the most precocious first day in mythology. Maia's child is born at dawn in a cave on Mount Cyllene; by midday he has found a tortoise, stretched gut-strings across its shell, and invented the lyre; by evening he slips out to Pieria and steals fifty of Apóllōn's cattle, driving them backward and binding brushwood to his own feet so the tracks deceive. myths.text: Zeús orders the cattle returned, and the confrontation on Mount Cyllene becomes the charter of exchange. Hermês offers the lyre; Apóllōn, hearing it, is enchanted, and trades the whole herd for the instrument, adding his golden staff and the gift of prophecy from the bee-maidens of Parnassus (Homeric Hymn 434–568). name: Hēphaistos

pronunciation: 'HEH-fye-stoss' — the first syllable carries the accent; the middle has a breathy 'ph' and a bright diphthong; the final syllable is crisp.
mythLead: Hēphaistos's myths turn disability into mastery. Thrown from heaven for being imperfect, he returns to Olympus as the indispensable artisan — and exacts, one masterpiece at a time, the recognition he was denied.

myths.title: Thrown from Olympus
myths.text: The sources disagree about who threw Hephaistos and why, and the disagreement is itself instructive. Hesiod's account has Hera bear him alone, in jealous rivalry of Zeus's parthenogenetic production of Athena — and reject the lame child (Theogony 927–929). The Iliad tells it from the smith's own mouth: it was Zeus who hurled him, when Hephaistos tried to shield Hera from the god's anger, and he fell 'all day long'…

mythLead: Selḗnē rules the night the way Hēlios rules the day — but where his light reveals, hers conceals, transforms, and bewitches. pronunciation: 'PSYCHE' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.
mythLead: Psychḗ runs the whole arc of the Greek soul: in Homer she is the breath that leaves the dying; in Plato the immortal charioteer; in Apuleius the heroine who weds Love and is made a goddess. Her story — the only complete divine romance to survive from antiquity — became the West's standing parable of the soul's trials.

myths.title: The Breath That Leaves

The Iliad sends Hector's psyche wailing down to Hades…

myths.title: The Oracle of the Mountain

The oracle of Milesian Apollo gives a monstrous answer: expose the girl on a mountain crag to wed a dire, fierce, serpent-like evil (Apuleius, Metamorphoses 4.32–33). mythLead: Venus’ mythology is Aphrodite’s retold in a Roman accent — the foam-birth, the Judgement of Paris, the loves and the intrigues — plus a Roman coda the Greeks never wrote: the divine ancestress of Rome. Virgil’s Aeneid makes her the poem’s moving force, the goddess who shields her son through Troy’s fall to Italy’s shore; and the Julian gens made her their household god.

myths.title: The Foam-Birth
myths.text: The Greek story: Cronus’ severed genitals fell into the sea, and from the foam (aphros) rose the goddess, first at Cyprus’ shore. Roman poets from Ennius onward retold it with Venus’ name — the sea-foam’s child Latinized without effort, the island of Cyprus keeping the cult’s oldest address.

myths.title: The Judgement of Paris
myths.text: At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the uninvited Strife threw the golden apple ‘to the fairest’ — and Hera, Athena, and Venus asked the shepherd Paris to judge. Venus’ bribe, Helen, won; the judgement’s price was Troy. The Roman telling keeps every detail — only the goddess’ name has changed, and the empire’s stake in the story.

myths.title: The Mother of the Race
myths.text: Virgil gives Venus her Roman apotheosis: she saves Aeneas from Troy’s burning, guides him through the sea-wanderings to Italy, and by the divine machinery’s decree founds the line — ‘I am Caesar and his whole Julian race’ — that will rule the world. No Greek goddess had such a son; the epic made her Rome’s mother.

She tells him of the golden age of the gods, the murder of Ymir, the creation of dwarves, and finally of Ragnarǫk: the wolf Fenrir's release, the serpent's rising, the darkening of the sun, and the fall of the gods.The poem dramatizes Óðinn's defining obsession: he already knows much, yet he cannot…

myths.title: The Eye in the Well of Mímir
myths.text: Beneath one root of Yggdrasill lies Mímir's well, in which wisdom and understanding are hidden, and Mímir is its keeper. Óðinn came to the well and asked for a single drink; the price was an eye. He pledged it, and Mímir took the eye and cast it into the well, where it still lies — so Snorri tells in Gylfaginning 15 — and ever after Óðinn sees with one eye in this world while his other gazes into the water of hidden…

myths.title: The Recovery of Mjölnir

They dressed Þórr in bridal linen and keys, hung the necklace Brísingamen on him, veiled his beard, and sent him east with Loki as his handmaid. At…

Þórr went with Týr to fetch it, slew Hymir's herd of oxen for dinner — the giant raged — and at dawn bullied him into a fishing trip, demanding the giant's best bait: the head of the fine ox Himinhrjóðr. Far out, Þórr rowed beyond the giant's comfort, hooked Jörmungandr, the world-serpent, and…

name: Loki

pronunciation: 'LOH-kee' — two even syllables with the weight on the first; keep the o short and round, and let the second syllable fall away lightly.
mythLead: Loki stands at the centre of more Eddic narrative than any figure save Þórr and Óðinn — and almost every road through the mythology crosses him at least once. The same wit that recovers Mjǫllnir in Þrymskviða engineers the death of Baldr; the Eddas hold both truths without reconciling them. By the giantess Angrboða he fathers Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr, and Hel; by his wife Sigyn, Nari and Váli, whose fates are spent in his own binding.

myths.title: The Blood-Brother

You said you would never taste ale unless it were brought to us both.' pronunciation: FRAY-ya — the first syllable is the diphthong ey, close to English 'ay' in 'say' with rounded lips; stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ja sounds like English 'ya'.
mythLead: Freyja is everywhere in the Norse corpus: the Poetic Edda, Snorri's prose, and the opening chapters of Heimskringla all circle her — her hall among the dead, her magic, her necklace, her lost husband, and the flyting in which Loki names her last.

myths.title: Fólkvangr and the Half of the Slain
myths.text: Snorri places Freyja beside Frigg as foremost among the goddesses, and gives her what no other goddess has: a share of the battle-dead. 'Her hall is called Sessrúmnir, and it is large and fair. Whenever she rides to battle, she takes half of the slain, and half belong to Óðinn.' Her field is Fólkvangr, the folk-plain; her hall is 'seat-roomy'. The Grímnismál preserves the same division in verse — Freyja chooses the…

myths.title: She Taught the Æsir Seiðr
myths.text: Heimskringla's euhemerized history makes Freyja the magic's transmitter: 'Freyja was a blótgyðja, a sacrificial priestess, and she was the first to teach the Æsir seiðr, which had been customary among the Vanir.' Seiðr — the far-reaching, fate-working magic that let its practitioner know the future and shape events — was Vanir craft, and it crossed into the Æsir's world through her; Ynglinga saga adds that Óðinn…

myths.title: The Hammer-Ransom
myths.text: When the giant Þrymr steals Mjölnir and names his price — Freyja as his bride — the gods bring her the offer. Her refusal is one of the Poetic Edda's great moments: 'Freyja was enraged, and snorted, so that the whole hall of the Æsir shook beneath her, and the great necklace of the Brísings burst: “You will know me to be most mad for a man, if I drive with you to the realm of the giants.”' No marriage happens.…

mythLead: Fenrir's mythology is a single arc told in two registers: Snorri's prose gives the binding in full narrative, while the poems — older, allusive, apocalyptic — carry the prophecy and the end. Together they make the most complete monster-story the North preserves: birth, fostering, fetters, pledge, gag, and the waiting that ends at Ragnarök.

Snorri names all three children of that union: the wolf Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr the world-serpent, and Hel, who is half the colour of the living and half of the dead. Because all were of giant stock and Loki's, and because the gods had heard prophecies that great harm would come of…

myths.title: Lœðingr and Drómi
myths.text: The wolf grew at a pace the gods could watch, and the prophecies grew plainer: he was fated to harm them. So the Æsir made a strong fetter called Lœðingr and brought it to the wolf, challenging him to test his strength against it. The wolf judged himself equal to it, let them bind him, braced himself, kicked — and the fetter sprang apart; he was loose from Lœðingr.The gods made a second fetter, half again as strong,…

Stronger than either iron fetter the wolf had snapped. At the isle of Lyngvi the gods showed him the band; suspicious, the wolf refused…

myths.title: Fimbulvetr: Three Winters Without a Summer
myths.text: The doom announces itself with weather. Völuspá 26 warns: 'a winter shall be great and fierce... snow will drive from all quarters, sharp frosts... three such winters will there be, with no summer in between.' Beneath the cold the moral world fails first: brothers kill brothers for gain, kinship is forgotten, 'woe is in the world, much whoredom, an axe-age, a sword-age, shields are cleft, a wind-age, a wolf-age,…

myths.title: The Breaking of Bonds
myths.text: When the winters end, every fetter fails at once. Fenrir — bound since the gods' fear outweighed their honor — snaps Gleipnir and gapes: his upper jaw touches the sky, his lower the earth. The Miðgarðsormr, released, churns the seas and floods the shore. Garmr, the hound before Gnipahellir, breaks loose and howls. Loki turns on the deck of the ship Naglfar — built, Snorri notes, from the fingernails and toenails of…

pronunciation: 'UEG-drah-sill' — the first vowel rounded like German ü, the double g and double l each held a fraction long, stress on the first syllable as in every Old Norse word.
mythLead: Yggdrasill has no adventures — it is the stage on which all adventures happen. The sources do not tell stories about the tree so much as they take attendance at it: the seeress sees it first, Óðinn hangs on it, the gods ride to it daily, the creatures live in it, and at the end of things it shudders and stands. The mythology of Yggdrasill is a set of sightings, each one from a different height of the cosmos.

myths.title: The Seeress's First Vision
myths.text: The seeress of Völuspá, reciting the world's history to [[odinn|Óðinn]], comes to the tree before almost anything else: 'An ash I know standing, called Yggdrasill, a high tree, sprinkled with white clay; from it come the dews that fall in the dales; it stands ever green over Urðr's well.' Earlier still she remembered nine worlds and the mjötviðr, the measuring tree, beneath the earth — the frame was there before the…

myths.title: Nine Nights on the Windy Tree
myths.text: Hávamál never names Yggdrasill, but the tradition has always read its most terrible stanzas onto it: 'I know that I hung on the windy tree nine whole nights, wounded by the spear, given to Óðinn, myself to myself, on that tree of which no man knows from what roots it rises.' No bread fed him, no horn refreshed him; he peered downward, took up the runes screaming, and fell back.The name itself is the commentary.…

name: Mjǫllnir

pronunciation: 'MYAWL-lnir' — begin with the mj of 'music', sound the vowel like the short rounded 'o' of 'hot', and hold the ll double before the final '-nir'.
mythLead: Mjǫllnir is the most famous weapon in the northern world and the busiest: no other treasure of the gods both kills and consecrates. Forged as the stake in one of Loki's wagers, it came out of Sindri's forge with a haft too short — and the gods judged it the best of all treasures anyway. The sources hand it four great stories: its flawed making, its theft, its duel, and its blessing of the dead god's pyre.

Swaggering, he wagers his head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri cannot make three finer treasures. At the forge, Loki becomes a fly and bites Brokkr at the bellows — arm, then neck, and Brokkr does not falter; but the third bite lands on his…

myths.text: Þórr wakes one morning and the hammer is gone. Loki borrows Freyja's falcon-shape, flies to Jötunheimr, and hears Þrymr boast that he has buried Mjǫllnir eight leagues down — and that no one recovers it unless Freyja is brought to him as bride. Freyja's refusal shakes her hall and snaps the necklace Brísingamen, so Heimdallr proposes the unthinkable: dress Þórr as the bride. The thunder-god protests — until Loki…

myths.text: The hammer's most dangerous duel came against the giant Hrungnir, who boasted in Asgard itself that he would kill all the gods, carry Freyja and Sif off to Jötunheimr, and drain the Æsir's ale. The gods sent for Þórr, and at the ford of Grjótúnagarðar the giant waited behind his stone shield, hurling his whetstone weapon. mythLead: The Osiris cycle is the best-preserved Egyptian myth, known from the Pyramid Texts onward: the good king murdered by his brother, the faithful wife who recovers him, the son who avenges him. It is simultaneously a story about kingship, about the flood that dies and returns, and about every human being who hoped to be judged worthy.

myths.title: The Death of the Good King
myths.text: The earliest sources already presuppose the story: Osiris ruled as a beneficent king until his brother Seth, envious of his power, contrived his death — in the classical telling (Plutarch’s De Iside et Osiride, the fullest narrative we have) sealed in a chest and thrown into the Nile, the river carrying him to Byblos where a tamarisk grew to engulf the coffin.

myths.title: Isis the Faithful
myths.text: Isis searched for the body, recovered it from Byblos, and hid it — but Seth found it by night, cut it into fourteen pieces, and scattered them through Egypt. Isis and Nephthys wandered the land gathering the fragments. Every place that claimed a fragment became an Osiris sanctuary; the myth is a map of Egyptian pilgrimage.

myths.title: The Weighing of the Heart
myths.text: Anubis conducts the dead to the Hall of Two Truths, where the heart is set on the scale against the feather of Maat and the tally is read aloud by Thoth. Wsjr, enthroned in the next chamber, receives those who pass. The formula “I am Osiris” in the Book of the Dead identifies the deceased with him — his resurrection becomes the template of theirs.

Set and Horus duel as hippopotami, charging to stay submerged three full months; Set proposes a night in one bed and is disgraced; Isis, disguised as a maiden, tricks Set into judging against himself; Horus, enraged at his mother's mediation, tears off…

mythLead: Amun's rise from provincial wind god to universal king is one of the great success stories of Egyptian religion. By the Middle Kingdom he is national; by the New Kingdom he is Amun-Ra, hidden lord of the cosmos; by the Late Period his oracles and priesthoods rival pharaonic power. His myths revolve around concealment, revelation, and the transmission of authority.

myths.text: Amun's beginnings are almost comically modest. His first attestations are Old Kingdom: in the Pyramid Texts he stands quietly beside his consort Amaunet among the eight 'Elder Gods' — the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, frog- and snake-headed powers of the primordial waters. He is a god of air and invisibility, one of eight, local to Thebes, a provincial town. Then history intervened. When the Theban dynasty of Mentuhotep II…

The sun-god's eye — his daughter, the fierce lioness — grows angry and flees south toward Nubia, and Egypt withers without her: crops fail, the Nile slackens, the gods' laughter stops. A messenger goes to bring her back; in the…

myths.title: Alexander at Siwa

Alexander the Great, having taken Egypt without a battle, crossed the Libyan desert to the oasis of Siwa, where Amun's oracle had spoken to Greeks for two centuries — Herodotus already knew Zeus Ammon of the oasis (Histories 2.42). name: Oṃ

mythLead: Oṃ has no biography, but it has a theology. Its “mythology” is the story of how a single syllable became the audible form of the absolute, repeated by gods, sages, and seekers across millennia — and defended, in the one tale the Upaniṣads tell about it, against every attempt to corrupt its channels.

myths.title: The Four-Footed Syllable
myths.text: The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, the shortest of the principal Upaniṣads, devotes itself entirely to a single syllable. Oṃ, it teaches, is the “imperishable” (akṣara), and it has four “feet” (pāda): the sound a is the waking state (vaiśvānara), the self outward-turned among gross things; u is the dream state (taijasa), inward-turned among subtle impressions; m is deep sleep (prājña), a mass of consciousness knowing neither…

myths.title: Oṃ and the Three Vedas
myths.text: The Chāndogya Upaniṣad identifies Oṃ as the essence of the three Vedas: just as all leaves are fastened to a single stalk, so all speech is fastened to this syllable, and “it is the quintessence of these essences, the highest of the high” (CU 1.1.8–10). The one who knows Oṃ obtains whatever he desires, for it is the doorway through which the Vedic hymns reach the gods; when two Brahmins dispute over the chant, it is…

myths.title: The Sacrifice of Sound
myths.text: In the Gītā, Kṛṣṇa declares himself among words by the syllable that begins Oṃ: “of imperishable things I am the syllable a” (Gītā 10.35), and instructs that acts of sacrifice, gift, and austerity begun with the three words oṃ tat sat are performed aright, for they were “fashioned of old from the utterance of oṃ” (17.23–24). The theology is practical before it is mystical: the one who abandons the body repeating Oṃ…

'Wide of stride did Viṣṇu stride out; three times he set down his footstep' (RV 1.154.2–3). In the Vedic dawn this is the sun's arc across the sky,…

mythLead: Sarasvatī's double biography — river first, word second — is the oldest story of how a landscape becomes a mind. The Ṛgveda knows her as a mighty stream of the heartland and, in the same breath, as Vāk, Speech itself. Between those two identities lies three thousand years of Indian civilization, which kept the name and forgot the water.

myths.title: Mightiest of Streams
myths.text: The Ṛgveda hymns her as a river of superlatives: 'purest in her course from the mountains to the sea,' whose might surpasses all other waters (RV 7.95; Nadīstuti, RV 10.75). The Nadīstuti hymn to the rivers sets her between the Yamunā and the Śutudrī — the heartland stream of the Vedic people — and names her 'best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses' in a single breath, collapsing geography, fertility, and…

myths.title: Vāk Speaks in the First Person
myths.text: Ṛgveda 10.125 is unique in the Veda: a hymn spoken by the goddess herself. 'I move with the Rudras, with the Vasus, with the Ādityas; I uphold Mitra and Varuṇa, Indra and Agni, and the two Aśvins... I am the queen, the gatherer of riches, the knowing one; the gods set me in many places, and many homes hold me. I breathe through all that breathes.' Vāk narrates her own supremacy: the gods perform their functions…

myths.title: Sarasvatī Fights for the Bharatas
myths.text: The Vedic Sarasvatī was no gentle muse. Ṛgveda 6.61 remembers her as a warrior stream of the Bharata clans: she 'destroyed the Pārāvatas' for her devotees and aided them in battle, while her turbulent floods smashed bridge and bank and bore off the poet's enemies (RV 6.61). The same hymn joins her name to Indra and to the twin Aśvins as a power to be summoned at the tribe's crisis. This is the goddess before her…

mythLead: Hanumān's mythology is drawn almost entirely from the Rāmāyaṇa, where he enters late and transforms everything: a minor forest-dweller who becomes the epic's decisive force. His stories are the anatomy of bhakti — what devotion can carry, leap, burn, and endure — and the reason the tradition made him the most beloved god of the North Indian street.

myths.title: The Wind's Son
myths.text: Hanumān's origin story is told by the old bear Jāmbavān, on the seashore before the great leap, when the vanaras doubted that anyone could cross the ocean (Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa 65–67, vulgate). As an infant, the child of the wind-god Vāyu and the vanara woman Añjanā saw the rising sun, mistook it for a ripe fruit, and leapt to eat it. Indra hurled his thunderbolt; it broke the child's jaw — hanu, the bone that…

myths.title: One Bound to Laṅkā
myths.text: When Sītā was carried across the ocean, the vanara army reached the shore and stopped: a hundred yojanas of water and no way across. The elder Jāmbavān reminded Hanumān of his strength; Hanumān grew until he filled the sky, pressed down on the mountain Mahendra with his foot, and leapt — clearing the ocean in a single bound (Rāmāyaṇa, Sundarakāṇḍa 1). He landed on Laṅkā's Trikūṭa hill, shrank himself to the size of…

myths.title: The Tail that Burned a City
myths.text: In Laṅkā, Hanumān let himself be taken — to measure the enemy, he said — and was dragged in his bonds before Rāvaṇa. Their exchange is one of the epic's great set-pieces: the captured monkey lecturing the ten-headed king on statecraft, diplomacy, and the certainty of his own destruction (Rāmāyaṇa, Sundarakāṇḍa 20–21). They attacked Brahmā himself as he sat upon the lotus rising from Viṣṇu's navel. myths.text: The buffalo-demon Mahiṣāsura had seized heaven through battle and austerity, and neither Brahmā, Viṣṇu, nor Śiva could defeat him. From their combined anger — from the gathered energy of all the gods — a blaze arose and took form: a woman with ten arms, three eyes, and a lion for her mount. Each god gave her a weapon: Śiva's trident, Viṣṇu's discus, Indra's thunderbolt, Yama's rod, Varuṇa's noose, Agni's spear…

name: Karma
tagline: Deed, Action, the Law of Consequence · Deed, action
domainGloss: Deed, Action, the Law of Consequence
pronunciation: “KAHR-muh”
mythLead: Karma has no biography because it outranks every biography: it is the rule all biographies obey. Its ‘mythology’ is the doctrine’s own history — from the Vedic ritual’s power to bind, through the Upaniṣads’ interiorization, to the great vehicles’ global export — and the countless stories, from Nala to Savitri, in which its arithmetic drives the plot.

myths.title: From Ritual to Moral Physics
myths.text: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad relocates karma: no longer the ritual act alone but the intention behind every act — ‘one becomes good by good action, evil by evil action’. The ritual economy of the Brahmins became the moral economy of the universe, and no priest was needed to run it.

myths.title: The Owner of the Deed
myths.text: The Buddha’s formula is the doctrine’s cleanest statement: beings are the owners of their deeds, the heirs of their deeds — nowhere else does the inheritance come from. Karma in Buddhism is intention (cetanā) itself; the deed’s fruit follows like the wheel follows the ox.

myths.title: The Story Where It Breaks
myths.text: The Mahābhārata’s Savitrī tale stages the doctrine’s limit-case: Satyavān’s life exhausted by karma’s count, Yama arrives on schedule — and the wife’s flawless speech wins the husband back. The epic never denies the law; it shows a love so exact in its dharma that the law’s own keeper must honour it.

mythLead: Cáishén's mythology is young and openly composite. The cult is a Song-dynasty growth over older roots, and every avatar brings his own story: a Ming novel supplies the marshal, a Han historian the heartless minister, merchants the retired sage. There is no canonical birth-story of Cáishén; instead, the office has been filled, again and again, by figures the culture wished to honor: a loyal minister, a canonized marshal, an honest merchant, even the red-faced war-god Guan Yu in some regions. During the fall of the Shang dynasty, Zhao Gongming, a hermit of Mount Emei, comes down to aid the doomed house with his black tiger, his iron whip, and his magic pearls; battle after battle turns on his power, until Jiang Ziya's side breaks him with Lu Ya's sorcery — an effigy of straw pierced by arrows. Bi Gan, uncle and chief minister of King Zhou of Shang, remonstrated against the tyrant's cruelties until the king, goaded on by his favorite Daji, ordered the minister's heart cut out — to test the old claim that a sage's heart has seven openings. tagline: The Two that Make the One
pronunciation: YIN-YAHNG — first syllable high and level, second syllable rising from mid to high.
mythLead: Yīnyáng has no origin myth in the usual sense. It is a lens through which Chinese thinkers read the origin of everything. Its stories are therefore cosmological and medical rather than biographical — a sequence of texts, from divination manual to Daoist classic to Han statecraft, each of which made the pair do more work.

myths.title: One Yin, One Yang
myths.text: The Xici — the Appended Statements, the philosophical commentary attached to the Yijing by the third century BCE — comes as close to a creed as the tradition allows: 'One yin and one yang: this is called the Dao' (Xici, Part A, §5). The cosmos, in this reading, is not governed by a personal deity but by the alternation of two modes, and the hexagrams of the classic are nothing more than snapshots of that alternation…

myths.title: All Things Carry Yin and Embrace Yang
myths.text: The Daodejing (ch. 42) compresses the whole cosmogony into nine characters of arithmetic: 'The Dao gives birth to One; the One gives birth to Two; the Two give birth to Three; the Three give birth to the ten thousand things.' Then it locates the pair inside every creature: 'The ten thousand things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang in their arms, and achieve harmony by blending the empty breath' (chongqi).…

myths.title: The Physician of Qin Reads the Six Qi
myths.text: By the sixth century BCE, yin-yang had become clinical. The Zuo Zhuan (Duke Zhao, year 1, 541 BCE) preserves what may be the first case history in Chinese literature: the ruler of Jin lies ill, and the court proposes ghosts and spoiled food as causes; the physician He, summoned from Qin, rejects both. Illness, he says, comes from the imbalance of the six qi of heaven — yin, yang, wind, rain, darkness, and light —…

Weary of the Zhou court's decay, the old archivist mounted a water buffalo and rode west toward the frontier. At Hán Gǔ Guān, the pass keeper Yīn Xī — who had divined that a sage would pass and had watched the sky for a purple vapor — recognized him and would not let him through without leaving a record.…

myths.title: The Rice-Cake That Flew
myths.text: The Nihon Shoki (Wadō 4, 711 CE) tells how Hata no Irogu, a leader of the immigrant Hata clan, practiced archery on a mountain by setting up a rice-cake as a target. When his arrow struck it, the cake rose into the air as a white bird and flew to the summit, where a radiance appeared. Taking this as a divine sign, Irogu founded a shrine on the spot. Rice-cake, white bird, mountain light: the kami announced itself…

myths.title: Three Gods, One Kami
myths.text: At its head shrine, Inari is not one deity but three: Uka-no-mitama, the spirit of the rice plant; Satahiko; and Ōmiyanome, the ancestral weaver and food-goddess. Other Inari shrines substitute Toyouke, the goddess of the Ise Grand Shrine's outer precinct, who prepares the food of the gods. Buddhist exegetes mapped the mountain as a lotus mandala, its ridges the lotus petals, its crater the heart of the world; ascending it was circumambulation and pilgrimage at once. The Lotus Sūtra's twenty-fifth chapter, the Universal Gateway, turns the etymology into a program: the Buddha declares that whoever calls Avalokiteśvara's name in the moment of terror — surrounded by fire, swept by flood, bound in chains, cornered by…

myths.title: Thirty-Three Forms for Every Kind of Suffering

Enkidu knows that wilderness and begs off — he has walked it — but goes for his friend's sake. The road is paved with dreams: each night the king climbs the mountain-pass to pray, and each dream…

At each of the seven gates the porter strips her of a garment or ornament — crown, beads, robe, until she stands naked before the throne of the dead. In the Enuma Elish she is first the generative mother of the divine generations, then the dragon-mother of monsters, and finally the cosmic body out of which Marduk fashions heaven and earth. She is not merely a sea; she is the possibility of both creation and destruction that precedes form.

From their mingling the divine generations rose like silt from a river's meeting: first Lahmu and Lahamu, then Anshar and Kishar, then the sky-god Anu, and finally Ea, the wisest of all. Ea struck first: he cast the slumber-spell on Apsû, slew him, and built his own house upon the corpse of the abyss. But the victory turned the mother. mythLead: The Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) is the central myth of Canaanite religion. It tells how Baꜥal wins kingship from the chaotic Sea, builds his palace, confronts Death, and returns to bring back the rains. In the opening tablets of the cycle (KTU 1.1–1.2), Ēl grants kingship to Yamm, the deified ocean, whose emissaries stride into the divine assembly and demand that Baꜥal himself be delivered as a captive. Baꜥal longs to strike the envoys down, but Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs restrains him: to kill the messengers would break the protocol of the gods. Instead the craftsman forges…

myths.title: The Cedar House on Zaphon

He sends ꜥAnat to plead before Ēl, but it is Asherah — the diplomatic wife of the old god — who finally secures the decree (KTU 1.4 iv–v). Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs raises a cedar palace on Mount Zaphon, the cosmic north mountain, and Baꜥal hosts the banquet of the gods. One decision troubles him: Kothar urges him to cut a window in the palace…

Baꜥal obeys: he takes his clouds, winds, and rains with him, and the earth dries behind him. You crushed the heads of Leviathan; you gave him as food for the creatures of the wilderness' (Psalm 74:12–17). The point is not that Leviathan is evil but that he is unmasterable by any human — only God can play with him…

name: Fionn
tagline: Hunter, Seer, Leader · Fair, white
pronunciation: 'FEEN' — one syllable; the f is slender and light, the vowel a long ee, the final nn broad against the teeth. 'Fionn mac Cumhaill' runs roughly 'FEEN mak KOO-il'.
mythLead: Fionn's cycle is the fullest hero-corpus Ireland kept: the Boyhood Deeds that make him wise, the Fenian lays and ballads that make him captain, and the two late romances — the pursuit of Diarmaid and the lay of Oisín — that make him tragic.

myths.title: The Boy in the Wild
myths.text: Fionn's father was Cumhall mac Trénmhóir, captain of the Fianna, who abducted Muirne, daughter of the druid Tadg, when her father refused her. Tadg's appeal brought the king's army, and Cumhall fell at the battle of Cnucha to Goll mac Morna, head of the rival Clann Morna. Muirne bore the child in danger and gave him to two women to rear in secret: Bodbmall the druidess and Liath Luachra the warrior-woman, who raised…

myths.title: The Salmon of Knowledge
myths.text: Demne came to learn poetry from Finn Éces, Finn the poet, who had waited seven years on the Boyne for the salmon of knowledge — the fish that had fed on the nuts of the nine hazels dropping into the well of Segais, so that all the knowledge of the world was in its flesh. When at last the salmon was caught, the poet set the boy to cook it and forbade him to taste any part of it. A blister rose on the fish's skin;…

Fionn came to Tara on Samain, and Fíacha mac Conga, who had served his father, gave him a magic spear and the instruction: hold its naked point to your forehead, and you will not sleep.…

name: Perun
tagline: Thunder, Lightning, Oak · Thunderer, striker
pronunciation: 'PER-un' with a rolled r; the name is an agent noun meaning 'Striker'.
mythLead: The stories of Perun survive mostly at second hand, through the chronicles of his enemies and the reconstructions of modern philologists. From them emerges a thunderer who is at once war-god and covenant-god: he hurls the bolt, he guards the sworn word, and he wages an eternal feud with Veles, lord of the underworld and the herd.

myths.title: Sworn by Their Own Weapons

Wandering volkhvy — sorcerers — declared that Perun had spoken: the powerful were hoarding grain while the common people starved, and the god demanded that the guilty be put to death. name: Quetzalcōātl
tagline: The Feathered Serpent
pronunciation: 'ket-SAHL-KOH-wahtl' — the 'tl' at the end is one sound, the 'z' is like 'ts,' and the whispered 'l' in 'zal' is Nahuatl ɬ.
mythLead: Quetzalcōātl's myths are not a single linear biography but a shifting constellation of roles: creator, priest-king, culture hero, exiled lord, and promised return. The narratives collected by Sahagún and other early colonial writers preserve the memory of a deity whose generosity and restraint are inseparable from his grief.

myths.title: The Fifth Sun from the Bones of the Old Age
myths.text: After the collapse of the Fourth Sun, the gods required a new humankind. Quetzalcōātl descended into Mictlān, the land of the dead, to ask Mictlantecuhtli for the bones of the previous races. The lord of the dead set a trap: Quetzalcōātl was to circle the underworld four times blowing a conch that had no holes. Quetzalcōātl had worms bore the shell and bees sound it from within, seized the bones, and fled; a quail…

myths.title: The Theft and Gift of Maize
myths.text: Maize, the flesh of humankind, was originally sealed inside Tonacatepetl, the Mountain of Our Sustenance, while the people of the Fifth Sun lived on bitter roots. Quetzalcōātl watched a red ant carrying a single kernel and followed it to the mountain's heart; taking the form of a black ant himself, he carried one grain back to the gods. myths.title: Ce Acatl Topiltzin at Tula

Under his rule, learning flourished, sacrifices were bloodless, and jade and quetzal feathers outnumbered obsidian blades. myths.title: The Canoe from Kahiki
myths.text: Pele came to Hawai'i from Kahiki — the ancestral homeland the Hawaiians left in the deep past — voyaging in a canoe with her brothers and sisters. Behind her she left a feud: her sister Nāmakaokaha'i, a sea goddess, held Pele to account for a seduction in the old country, and the ocean pursued the canoe across the archipelago. At island after island Nāmaka caught up, and Pele's fires were quenched in steam; in the…

myths.title: The Digging Stick Pā'oa
myths.text: From island to island Pele dug with her sacred digging stick Pā'oa, sinking deep pits in search of a fire-pit the sea's creatures could not kill. Kaua'i, O'ahu, the channels of Maui — at each, the water found her out and drove her on, the steam of her drowning fires rising as the islands' mists. At last, on the great island of Hawai'i, she sank her pit into the flank of Kīlauea, and the sea could not reach it. There…

myths.title: Hi'iaka and the Chief of Kaua'i
myths.text: Pele's youngest sister, Hi'iaka-i-ka-poli-o-Pele, was her favorite — kept in her bosom, raised as guardian of the hula. Gazing in vision across the sea, Pele fell in love with Lohi'au, a chief of Kaua'i, and sent Hi'iaka to fetch him with power and a strict command: a set term, and do not embrace him. His capital was at Koso, and his cult grew from the worship of a deified king: subsequent Aláàfins ruled as his heirs, and the Ṣàngó festival at Ọ̀yọ́…

myths.title: The Fire That Consumed the Palace
myths.text: Johnson's chronicle credits Ṣàngó with a fearful sorcery: charms that breathed fire on his enemies. In the most told episode, his own overreaching turned the weapon inward — the fire that burned his foes spread through his palace and his household, and the king who had terrorised Ọ̀yọ́ with thunder-magic died, or fled, by the same element (Johnson 1921; Law 1977 treats the traditions with scholarly reserve). The sixteenth-century chroniclers — Betanzos, Sarmiento de Gamboa, Murúa, and later Cobo — preserve the state myths that made a mountain people the children of the sun: a creator who sired the daystar, a brother and sister sent to found Cuzco, and a solstice festival that renewed the world each year.

Two spirits stood forth there, twins — Spenta Mainyu, the Holy Creative Spirit, and Angra Mainyu, the Destructive — 'the better and the bad in thought, word, and deed' (Yasna 30.3–5). myths.title: The Seven Creations and the Assault of Ahriman
myths.text: In the Pahlavi Bundahišn, AhuraMazdā creates the world in seven successive acts: first the sky as a round shell, then water, then earth, then plants, then the sole primordial bull, then Gayōmart the first man, and finally fire — 'the life of all creation' (Bundahišn 1–3).
